title: Unreliable Plotter
pitch: A virtual pen plotter draws a generative poster line by line on screen: flow-field ribbons and spiral-packed circles (plus L-system shrubs if time allows), each in two or three pens. A mishap dial lets the machine misbehave in stylised ways (a pen drying out and skipping, a blot on touchdown, paper creeping between pen swaps), narrated by a deadpan operator log. The visitor hunts for the dial setting where the imperfections make the poster better than the ideal version, then shares the seed or saves the layered SVG.
whyNow: Timeless: pen-plotter flow-field art is an established craft scene, and the page treats machine error as a creative parameter.

research.summary: A flow field is a grid of direction vectors, usually angles taken from Perlin noise, along which particles are traced to produce smooth curves; each curve is one continuous stroke, which suits a plotter. Plotter tooling such as vpype treats each SVG layer as one pen, so the page exports layers per pen. The mishap model is stylised: ordinary pens skip when the tip is clogged by dried ink or paper fibres, but the page does not claim any calibration to a specific plotter. Paper drift during long plots and offsets at pen swaps are reported only in forum anecdotes and one patent that calls pen-drag shift usually negligible, so the page presents them as playful exaggeration, not measured fact. Perlin's paper 'An Image Synthesizer' appeared at SIGGRAPH in 1985; sources disagree on when the noise was first developed, so the page leaves that date out.

facts.claim: A flow field is a grid of direction vectors; Perlin noise is a common way to choose the angles, and particles traced along the field give smooth curves.
In plotter tooling such as vpype, each SVG layer holds the geometry for one pen or colour, and vfab maps detected layers to pens.
Ordinary pens skip when the tip is clogged by dried ink or lodged paper fibres; the page borrows this as a stylised model, not a plotter calibration.
Perlin's paper 'An Image Synthesizer' appeared in Computer Graphics (SIGGRAPH) in 1985.

design.coreLoop: Pick a composition and a seed, press plot, and watch the pen draw in real time while the operator log narrates events. The mishap dial changes how often ink skips, blots appear, the paper creeps or a pen swap lands slightly off. An ideal-versus-actual ghost toggle shows what the machine meant to draw, so each seed becomes a small experiment and finding the dial setting that flatters a given composition is the goal.
sophisticationHooks: Seeded composition engines (flow-field ribbons with spacing control and spiral-packed circles; L-system shrubs as a stretch) split across 2 to 3 pen layers

Stylised machine model: ink reservoir that depletes with distance and recovers on re-dip, touchdown blots, cumulative paper creep that misregisters later layers, with all randomness drawn from the seed so the URL reproduces the same plot
Operator log with deadpan one-line entries per event and an ideal-versus-actual ghost overlay
Exports: layered SVG of the ideal paths (labelled as ideal) and a PNG of the as-plotted poster with a plot-number caption
design.scopeForOneDay: Must ship: two composition engines (flow-field ribbons, spiral-packed circles), plotter-state model in a worker, canvas2d renderer with per-pen ink look, playback controls (speed, pause, skip to end), mishap dial plus 3 individual toggles (dry pen, blot, paper creep), operator log, ideal-vs-actual ghost, hash state (composition, seed, pens, dial), SVG and PNG export through Blob downloads, light and dark paper themes, reduced-motion path (instant draw), short about panel. Stretch only if QA slack remains: L-system engine, pen-swap offset toggle. Cut: real G-code, stepper-motor audio, user-drawn input paths.
risks: The mishap physics is stylised and not calibrated to a real machine; the UI says so.

Unverified: the claim that a plotter can only draw lines and cannot cover earlier ink (Hobbs essay) could not be found again; the page omits it or shows it as 'as of 2026-10-10, per a search result for Tyler Hobbs's plotter essay, unconfirmed'.

Unverified: paper creep over long plots rests on forum anecdotes (one Signs101 thread) and pen-swap offsets on an unattributed anecdote; the page presents both as playful exaggeration and says 'reported by hobbyists, not measured', or omits them.
Ordinary-pen skipping sources are not plotter-specific, so the about panel presents them as inspiration only.
Performance: long plots can reach tens of thousands of segments, so segments are batched, capped (about 60k) and drawn incrementally to a backing canvas.
Dial and toggle count could crowd a 360px layout; the controls fold into a drawer on small screens.
Flow-field ribbons are a very familiar look; differentiation relies on the machine-error layer and log, which needs strong writing and visible payoffs where ideal and actual differ clearly.

verification.notes: Core technique and layer-per-pen workflow were found again in independent search results; no page could be opened, and the plotter-constraint and paper-creep claims stay unverified and are softened. Buildable offline in a morning once scoped to two engines.
